description: We are a driven, cross-disciplinary team, competing in The Space Apps Comp. We are very passionate about space exploration, satellite visualisation of data, environmental science, and building practical technology solutions using NASA’s open-source data. We don’t want to simply build a prototype for the competition, but build an impactful, scalable project that addresses real-world challenges on Earth or in space.
summary:
POLARIS is an interactive lunar mission planning and landing site assessment tool we created for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. Landing site assessment on the Lunar South Pole was complicated due to the low solar grazing incidence angle (~1.5⁰ above the lunar horizon), Direct-to-Earth (DTE) line of sight, high incline crater walls and Proximity to Permanently Shadowed Regions. The process is further hindered by the lack of integration between many tools causing slow processing.

Using NASA LRO LOLA topography data and SPICE/DE440 planetary ephemeris, POLARIS takes 235,777 points across a 100 x 100 kilometer area of the South Pole. Tables are pre-calculated and parallelised using Numba to quickly create complete 30 day suitability maps in 2.2 seconds. Data has been validated against NASA LOLA solar illumination maps (0.988 correlation) and JPL Horizons (0.005" error). Calculations include: solar masking angles of up to 250 kilometers, lander battery usage for each hour, and a 3D terrain flyover. This tool allows mission planners, scientists and educators to make quick data driven Go/No-Go decisions.
details:
WHAT POLARIS DOES

Polaris (https://nsa.palantyr.org/) takes raw data of lunar topography and orbital dynamics, and creates an intuitive interface that allows users to optimise their mission by inputting mission dates, spacecraft limitations and prioritising objectives. Based on this, it creates a prioritised Flight Plan:

1) Hybrid high-resolution grid (235,777 points): An initial uniform grid (160000 points) is created for the lunar south pole region (100x100km = 10,000km^2) with a resolution of 250m. This is supplemented with targeted points (75,777 points). These points are taken from the local topographical peak, taking a ±40m radius around each peak. Finally the grid has been refined with a 50m grid in high-illumination regions ensuring all thin illuminated ridges are captured.

2) 360-720 degree Horizon Ray-casting: Using NASA LOLA’s Digital Elevation Models (20m and 80m resolutions) Polaris calculates the amount of horizon blocked from the observer at 2m from the surface. This is done for 360 different directions (1 degree increments) up to 250km away. The results are then refined using 720 different directions (0.5 degree increments).

3) Ephemeris & Power: Using NASA NAIF’s SPICE (DE440) code Polaris calculates precise vectors to the Sun and Earth, including lunar libration. A basic lander power system is then simulated (Solar panel: 2m^2 with 28% efficiency, Battery: 2000Wh, Active Load: 120W, Sleep Load: 35W and Wake-up Load: When battery level below 20%, Sleep Load will be used until battery reaches 30%).

4) Trajectory & 3D: Lunar transfer trajectories are calculated from the Earth to Moon to ensure accuracy. These have been verified using patched conics and 3-body numerical integration (Earth-Moon-Sun). Interactive 3D models are created using Three.js.

5) Prioritisation & Robustness: Slopes above 10 degrees are filtered. Remaining suitable sites are given a score out of 100 based on weights. Sites are also required to be at least 1.5km apart if they are within the top 5 recommendations. If the mission cannot meet the requirements, requirements will be relaxed (25% -> 50% -> No Limitations). However, the slope is still limited to =<10 degrees.

BENEFITS

Fast re-planning of launch delays. By pre-calculating the static horizon for topography data (1 hour on 16 threads) and storing the last 6 date ranges using Numba compiled loops and variable time steps (Δt = max(1, ceil(24D/400)) hours) we can calculate 30 days worth of suitability in 2.2 seconds on a 16 thread machine or 15-30 seconds on a 2 core server. The prioritisation can be re-calculated in 1-2 seconds.

Better alignment between science and engineering. Ensures geologists are able to target water ice in the Permanently Shadowed Regions (PSR) while still protecting engineers with safety requirements such as thermal conditions, battery charging and DTE connections.

Easy to understand. Converts complicated polar geometry and lunar libration into easy to understand maps and 3D.

TOOLS & LANGUAGES

Science & backend: Python, Numba (Just-In-Time Parallel Compilation), SpiceyPy (NASA NAIF, SPICE Kernels (DE440)), NumPy & SciPy.

Front End: Web app (https://nsa.palantyr.org/) using Three.js/WebGL. Creates 3D models of LOLA.

Test suite: 181 science & API unit tests, 97 browser tests.

CREATIVE & ENGINEERING VALIDATION

Local sensitivity: It was shown that moving the landing site by only 100m will cause 7 of the 8 surrounding points to not meet mission requirements. This shows that re-calculating local points is essential.

Validated by NASA: Calculations for the position of the Sun & Earth agree with JPL Horizons to within 0.005". Calculations for solar illumination agree with NASA LOLA (r=0.988). Calculations for Earth visibility agree with NASA LOLA (r=0.991). PSR agrees with 99.5% accuracy.

Considered factors for polar missions: The grazing incidence of the sun at ~1.5 degrees, Permanently Shadowed Regions (-200°C), Radio blackouts due to ridges and libration, Lander slope limited to =<10 degrees, Battery survival when sleeping/waking and Multi-day calculations.
